title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Appropriate Equipment & Instrumentation - Biotechnology - Total magnification, oil immersion
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: A microbiologist is observing a Gram-stained smear of *E. coli* utilizing a standard brightfield compound microscope. They are looking through standard $10\times$ ocular eyepieces and have rotated the turret to engage the high-power $40\times$ objective lens. What is the **total optical magnification** of the final image reaching the observer's retina?
questions.explain:
Total magnification in a compound microscope is calculated by multiplying the magnification power of the **ocular lens (eyepiece)** by the power of the **objective lens**. 

$$ \text{Total Magnification} = 10\times (\text{Ocular}) \times 40\times (\text{Objective}) = 400\times $$ 
At this magnification, the image appears $400$ times larger than its actual size.

questions.q: When attempting to observe individual bacterial cells, a technician must rotate the turret to the $100\times$ objective lens and place a single drop of immersion oil directly between the glass slide and the lens. What is the fundamental optical physics principle behind utilizing this specialized oil?
options: The oil shares the same refractive index as glass, preventing the light rays from scattering or bending outward as they pass through the air gap, thus capturing more light into the narrow objective lens.
The oil inherently acts as a secondary fluid convex lens, magically providing a direct $10\times$ multiplicative boost to the magnification.
The oil physically cools the fragile glass slide by dissipating the intense heat generated by the halogen lamp.
The oil selectively absorbs and filters out the blue wavelengths of light, drastically increasing the structural contrast of Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.explain:
The resolution of a microscope at extreme magnifications is severely limited by the refraction (bending) of light as it transitions from the glass slide into the less dense air. 

**Immersion oil** has roughly the exact same **refractive index** ($\approx 1.51$) as the glass slide and the objective lens. By creating a continuous physical bridge of oil, the light rays travel straight through the slide, into the oil, and up into the lens without scattering, which massively increases the resolution and clarity of the image at $1000\times$ total magnification.

questions.q: Following a microscopy session using the $100\times$ oil immersion objective, strict optical care protocols dictate that the lens must be immediately and thoroughly cleaned. Which material represents the **only** acceptable item a technician should use to wipe the immersion oil off the objective lens?
options: A standard laboratory paper towel moistened lightly with warm, deionized water.
A coarse industrial Kimwipe specifically engineered for scrubbing acidic benchtop spills.
High-quality, non-abrasive optical lens paper, utilized either dry or with specialized lens cleaning solution.
A highly concentrated $70\%$ ethanol wipe commonly used to sterilize biological safety cabinets.
questions.explain:
Microscope objective lenses feature incredibly delicate, highly engineered optical anti-reflective coatings. 

Using paper towels, bench wipes, or aggressive solvents will easily scratch these microscopic coatings and permanently ruin the optical clarity of a very expensive lens. The **only** appropriate material for cleaning microscope optics is specially manufactured **lens paper**, optionally paired with a manufacturer-approved optical lens cleaning fluid.
